country.evidence_source: [page/7/Text/5] Table 3 shows results of testing two structural models of the relationship between optimism and the components of general SWB. Both models had a reasonable fit to data in all three samples according to fit indices. The comparison between Model 1 (total mediation via affectivity) and Model 2 (the full cognitive-affective model with a direct path between optimism and global life satisfaction) favored Model 2. Although there were only marginal differences in RMSEA and AGFI between the models, however Model 2 had a lower AIC and the chi-square decreased significantly in all three samples with the highest drop for the Lithuanian sample (\Delta \chi^2 = 27.19, \Delta df = 1, p < .01) as compared to the Swedish sample at two time points (\Delta \chi^2 = 19.08 and \Delta \chi^2 = 12.31, both \Delta df = 1 and p < .01, at age 43 and 49, respectively).

Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [page/7/Text/5] Table 3 shows results of testing two structural models of the relationship between optimism and the components of general SWB. [page/7/Text/6] Figure 1 shows that in the Swedish sample, both at age 43 and age 49, optimism influenced GLS both directly and indirectly via affect whereas in the Lithuanian sample an indirect affect was very low. [page/7/Text/9] In accordance to Carver and Scheier's (2002b) notion that optimists vs. pessimists tend to generate and experience more positive vs. negative feelings, the results indicated strong direct effect of optimism on PA and NA in both samples.
